stem: A Nash equilibrium is a set of strategies in which:
choices: Players can improve by changing together
No player can improve his or her payoff by unilaterally changing strategy
Each player uses a dominant strategy
Both players get their highest possible payoff
explain: Slide p. 32. It need not be the best outcome, and players need not have dominant strategies.

stem: True or false: A Nash equilibrium is always the outcome that gives the players the highest combined payoff.
explain: False. In the Visa game the equilibrium (2, 2) is worse for both than (3, 3).

stem: True or false: A game can have more than one pure-strategy Nash equilibrium.
In the underline method, a cell is a Nash equilibrium when:
choices: At least one number is underlined
Its first number is the largest in the matrix
Both numbers in it are underlined as best responses
explain: Each player must be best-responding to the other.

stem: Visa and Mastercard would both be better off maintaining fees. Why can't they agree to do so in a one-shot game?
choices: Each has an incentive to defect from the agreement
explain: Slide p. 36: both would have an incentive to defect.

stem:
Visa (rows) and Mastercard (columns), from the slides:

| Visa \ Mastercard | Lower | Maintain |
|---|---|---|
| Lower | 2, 2 | 4, 1 |
| Maintain | 1, 4 | 3, 3 |

What is the Nash equilibrium?
explain: Both have the dominant strategy Lower, so (Lower, Lower) = (2, 2). At (Maintain, Maintain) each could switch to Lower and get 4.

stem:
Dillard's (rows) and Nordstrom (columns), from the in-class exercise:

| Dillard's \ Nordstrom | Girl's | Women's |
|---|---|---|
| Girl's | 2, 1 | 4, 2 |
| Women's | 6, 4 | 3, 5 |

What is the Nash equilibrium?
explain: Nordstrom's dominant strategy is Women's; Dillard's best response is Girl's (4 > 3). Check Nordstrom: given Girl's, Women's 2 > 1.

stem:
Firm X (rows) and Firm Y (columns):

| X \ Y | Left | Right |
|---|---|---|
| Top | 8, 3 | 12, 9 |
| Bottom | 5, 6 | 4, 2 |

What is the Nash equilibrium?
explain: Top is dominant for X (8 > 5, 12 > 4). Y's best response to Top is Right (9 > 3).

stem:
Player A (rows) and Player B (columns), textbook Table 10-1:

| A \ B | Left | Right |
|---|---|---|
| Up | 10, 20 | 15, 8 |
| Down | -10, 7 | 10, 10 |

What is the Nash equilibrium?
explain: Up is dominant for A (10 > -10, 15 > 10). B's best response to Up is Left (20 > 8).

stem:
Row (rows) and Column (columns), a 3 by 3 game:

| Row \ Column | Left | Center | Right |
|---|---|---|---|
| Top | 4, 3 | 5, 1 | 6, 2 |
| Middle | 2, 1 | 8, 4 | 3, 6 |
| Bottom | 3, 0 | 9, 6 | 2, 8 |

What is the Nash equilibrium?
explain: Underline: Row's best vs Left is Top (4), vs Center Bottom (9), vs Right Top (6). Column's best vs Top is Left (3), vs Middle Right (6), vs Bottom Right (8). Only (Top, Left) has both.

stem:
How many pure-strategy Nash equilibria does this game have?

| Firm A \ Firm B | USB-C | Proprietary |
|---|---|---|
| USB-C | 40, 40 | 5, 5 |
| Proprietary | 5, 5 | 40, 40 |
explain: (USB-C, USB-C) and (Proprietary, Proprietary): matching is each firm's best response.

stem:
How many pure-strategy Nash equilibria does the employee monitoring game have?

| Boss \ Employee | Work | Shirk |
|---|---|---|
| Monitor | -1, 1 | 1, -1 |
| Don't Monitor | 1, -1 | -1, 1 |
explain: Every cell has one player who wants to switch, so there is no pure equilibrium. Players randomize.

stem: Two coffee chains each pick a new store location: Downtown or Campus. Each earns 5 if they pick different spots and 2 if they pick the same spot. Which outcomes are Nash equilibria?
explain: If the rival is Downtown, your best is Campus (5 > 2), and vice versa. Splitting up is stable either way.

stem: In a Nash equilibrium, a manager says, "We could earn more if our rival changed its price." Does that mean the outcome is not a Nash equilibrium?
choices: No; Nash equilibria require both players to earn the same
Yes; any player who could earn more means no equilibrium
No; Nash only requires that no player gains by changing ITS OWN strategy
explain: The test is unilateral deviation, not whether a better outcome exists.

stem:
Game Theory Exercise Part 1 (payoffs in $ millions, Facebook, Twitter):

| Facebook \ Twitter | Ban | Don't Ban |
|---|---|---|
| Ban | -350, -3 | -350, 23 |
| Don't Ban | -277, -3 | -280, -12 |

What is the Nash equilibrium?
explain: Facebook's Don't Ban is dominant; Twitter's best response to it is Ban (-3 > -12).

stem:
Game Theory Exercise Part 3 (regulation risk 15% if both don't ban, 5% if only one doesn't):

| Facebook \ Twitter | Ban | Don't Ban |
|---|---|---|
| Ban | -350, -3 | -350, 29 |
| Don't Ban | -137, -3 | -420, -18 |

How many pure-strategy Nash equilibria are there?
choices: Two: (Ban, Don't Ban) and (Don't Ban, Ban)
explain: Each firm's best response is the opposite of its rival's: Facebook -350 > -420 and -137 > -350; Twitter 29 > -3 and -3 > -18.
